Family Health

Cystoscopy: why it is done and what to expect

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A cystoscopy lets a specialist look inside the bladder and urethra. Knowing why it is being done, what else may happen during the visit and how to recover can make the appointment easier to plan.

What cystoscopy can show

Cystoscopy is an examination of the bladder and urethra, the passage through which urine leaves the body. The instrument is called a cystoscope: a narrow tube with a light and viewing system. It lets the clinician inspect the lining directly, usually using images on a screen.

A referral may follow blood in the urine, repeated urinary infections, persistent burning, troublesome urgency or frequency, difficulty emptying, or some forms of pelvic pain. These symptoms have several possible causes. Cystoscopy is not automatically needed for every infection or for uncomplicated overactive bladder.

The examination may identify a bladder stone, a growth, inflammation, narrowing or signs of obstruction associated with an enlarged prostate. A growth is not automatically cancer: a tissue sample may be needed to establish what it is. The reason for the test should be explained in terms of the question it is intended to answer.

An examination can include sampling or treatment

Small instruments can pass through a cystoscope to take a biopsy, treat bleeding or remove selected stones or abnormal tissue. Some procedures also allow urine to be collected for laboratory testing. The exact work depends on the equipment, setting and agreed plan; a diagnostic appointment does not imply that every problem will be treated immediately.

Cystoscopy may be part of placing or removing a ureteric stent, a small tube used to help urine drain between a kidney and the bladder. It can also provide access for a retrograde pyelogram, in which contrast dye and X-rays show parts of the upper urinary tract.

Looking into the bladder does not itself inspect the entire kidneys and ureters. Ureteroscopy uses a different instrument to reach farther up that system. Ask whether your appointment involves only cystoscopy, an additional imaging test or another treatment, and discuss the benefits and risks before giving consent.

Flexible and rigid scopes have different roles

A flexible cystoscope bends and is commonly used for an outpatient inspection. A rigid cystoscope is straight and is often chosen when more substantial treatment is planned. The choice is made for the task and the person, not because one type is always better.

A small biopsy can sometimes be taken with a flexible instrument. It is therefore inaccurate to assume that any tissue sample requires a rigid scope or a general anaesthetic. Conversely, finding something during a flexible examination may lead to a separate treatment appointment.

A straightforward flexible examination often takes around ten to fifteen minutes, while rigid procedures may take about half an hour or longer depending on the work. Registration, preparation and recovery add time. Ask about the whole visit when arranging transport, childcare or time away from work.

Prepare the medicine and infection plan

The team may request a urine sample before the examination. Tell them about new burning, fever or other possible infection symptoms. An active infection may need treatment first, and the appointment may be rescheduled. Preventive antibiotics are selected according to the procedure and infection risk; they are not a universal requirement before and after every cystoscopy.

Bring a list of prescriptions, non-prescription medicines and supplements, and mention allergies or previous problems with anaesthesia. Blood thinners and some other medicines may affect bleeding or preparation. Do not stop them yourself: ask the team and the prescriber for a clear plan.

If you have diabetes, a weakened immune system, fluid restrictions or a possibility of pregnancy, mention this beforehand. A practical written plan should tell you what to take, when to eat or drink, whether to arrive with a urine sample or a comfortably full bladder, and whom to call if your health changes.

Understand the anaesthetic and arrange help

Local anaesthetic gel numbs and lubricates the urethra while you remain awake. For a simple flexible examination, eating and drinking normally is usually possible. Follow your own appointment instructions if a different plan has been made.

A general anaesthetic puts you to sleep. A spinal anaesthetic is given through the lower back and numbs the lower part of the body; it does not necessarily make you unconscious. Sedation may sometimes be used for comfort, but it has its own recovery and driving restrictions.

General or spinal anaesthesia usually involves additional preparation and time in recovery. Follow the precise fasting instructions rather than guessing a number of hours. Arrange the required escort and adult support at home; being technically awake afterward does not mean your judgement, coordination or mobility has fully recovered.

What happens during the examination

You may first be asked to pass urine, sometimes into a sample container. Staff provide privacy to change into a gown and help you lie on the examination couch, with your legs positioned as needed. The team checks the agreed procedure and makes sure the anaesthetic plan is working.

The clinician gently passes the lubricated scope through the urethra into the bladder. Sterile saline expands the bladder enough to see its lining. You may notice pressure, brief stinging or a strong urge to urinate as it fills. You can ask what is happening, and some clinics let you watch the images.

Tell the clinician if you have significant pain or need a pause. Any sampling or treatment should follow the agreed consent plan. At the end, the instrument is removed and the fluid is drained or passed as urine. The team should explain what was actually done before you leave.

Mild after-effects should improve

Some people notice mild burning, more frequent trips to the toilet or a small amount of blood in the urine afterward, particularly after a biopsy. These effects should settle rather than become progressively worse. The expected duration differs with the procedure, so use your discharge advice and contact the team if symptoms persist beyond the period they described.

Drink according to the advice you receive and any heart or kidney-related fluid restriction. Do not force large volumes of water to try to clear heavy bleeding or an inability to urinate. Pass urine when you need to rather than deliberately holding a painful full bladder.

A comfortably warm, damp cloth near the urethral opening may ease discomfort. Ask which pain relief is suitable: paracetamol may be an option, while ibuprofen is not right for everyone. Follow the label or prescription and do not add medicines that conflict with your existing treatment.

Know which symptoms need prompt help

Infection, significant bleeding, urinary retention and injury are possible complications, although serious problems are uncommon. Swelling can sometimes make it difficult to empty the bladder and a temporary urinary catheter may be needed. Do not assume that every worsening symptom is an expected part of recovery.

Get urgent help if you cannot urinate and your lower abdomen feels full, swollen or painful. There is no need to wait eight hours when you are uncomfortable and unable to empty. Heavy bleeding, bright red urine or clots, severe abdominal pain, fever or chills also need prompt assessment.

New back or flank pain, nausea, worsening burning and feeling generally unwell may accompany an infection. An unusual urine smell alone is not a diagnosis, but report it with other symptoms. If you are very unwell, seek emergency care rather than waiting for a routine callback.

Return to activity according to what was done

After an uncomplicated flexible examination with local anaesthetic, you may be able to resume ordinary activities when comfortable. A biopsy, stone treatment or other intervention can change that advice. Rest if you need it and keep the contact number and discharge information accessible.

After general or spinal anaesthesia, the NHS advises an adult to take you home and stay for twenty-four hours, with no driving, alcohol or heavy machinery during that period. Sedation also requires specific restrictions. Follow your service’s instructions if they are longer or differ for your situation.

Ask separately about exercise, heavy lifting, work and sex. A blanket two-week ban is not appropriate for every cystoscopy, but it may be part of a particular treatment plan. If a stent or catheter remains, confirm how to care for it and when it will be removed or reviewed.

Make sure you receive the findings and next steps

The clinician may describe visible findings immediately. A biopsy or urine test needs laboratory analysis, so a complete answer can take longer. Ask when the result is expected, how it will reach you and who is responsible for following it up.

If you were sedated, it can help to have the explanation written down or shared with your chosen support person. Keep a note of any medicines, activity limits and planned appointments. Contact the service if the promised result does not arrive.

A normal-looking bladder is useful information, but it does not explain every possible urinary symptom or exclude conditions elsewhere. Ask whether further urine tests, imaging or symptom treatment are needed. The purpose of the visit is a clear next step, not simply completing the procedure.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Preparation depends on the scope, anaesthetic and any treatment planned.

A flexible scope can sometimes take a small biopsy.

Inability to urinate with a painful full bladder needs urgent care.

How BeMama can help

Before the appointment, write down the reason for the test, the medicine plan, the ride-home arrangements and the contact for results.

When to seek help

Seek urgent help for painful inability to urinate, heavy bleeding or clots, fever, severe pain or feeling very unwell after the procedure.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Ask what question the examination is meant to answer.
  • Do not stop blood thinners without an agreed plan.
  • Antibiotics and fasting are not identical for every procedure.
  • Mild symptoms should improve, not worsen.
  • Confirm how biopsy results and follow-up will be provided.

Frequently asked questions

Is cystoscopy the same as the cystoscope?

No. Cystoscopy is the procedure; the cystoscope is the instrument used to look inside.

Does a referral mean I have bladder cancer?

No. It may investigate several symptoms and conditions. Any abnormal tissue may need laboratory testing before a diagnosis is made.

Can a flexible cystoscopy include a biopsy?

Yes. Small samples can sometimes be taken with a flexible scope; the team will explain whether this is part of your plan.

Must everyone fast before the test?

No. A simple flexible examination often allows normal food and drink, while other anaesthetic plans require specific fasting instructions.

Should I stop my blood thinner?

Only if the treating team and prescriber give you a clear plan. Do not stop it on your own.

Will I be asleep?

Local gel, spinal anaesthesia, general anaesthesia and sometimes sedation have different effects. Ask which you are having.

Is a little blood in the urine expected?

It can occur after the examination, especially after sampling. Heavy bleeding, clots, worsening symptoms or persistent bleeding needs advice.

Should I wait eight hours if I cannot urinate?

No. A painful or swollen full bladder with inability to urinate needs urgent help.

Must I avoid lifting for two weeks?

Not after every cystoscopy. Restrictions depend on any biopsy or treatment, so follow your discharge plan.

When will the result be ready?

Visible findings may be discussed immediately. Biopsy and urine results need laboratory time; ask when and how to expect them.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
